lesson_title: The Answer You Threw in the Bin: Solving Quadratic and Exponential Equations
hook_text: x squared equals five x. You wrote x equals five. You just binned half the marks.
clip_script: Here is a fact about money you already believe. A stall's takings are the price times the number sold. If the takings are R0, either the price was zero, or she sold nothing. There is no third story. But if the takings were R60? Could be anything. That is why zero is the only number that talks — and why every quadratic gets pushed until one side reads zero before you factorise. Now the bin. x squared equals five x. Almost everyone divides both sides by x and writes x equals five. Not wrong — but not whole, because zero is a solution too. Put zero in: zero equals zero. True. Dividing by x quietly assumed x was not zero, and threw that answer away. Do it safely: x squared minus five x equals zero. Take out the common factor: x, times x minus five, equals zero. So x is zero, OR x is five. Both kept. New permanent rule: never divide an equation by anything containing the unknown. Factorise instead. Dividing destroys answers. Factorising keeps them.
visual_style: A busy street stall: a till reading R0 beside a till reading R60, then an x quietly dropping into a bin and being fished back out as the factorised line assembles.
pacing: Warm setup on the takings, a sharp beat at the bin, firm and clean on the rule.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson and stop giving away roots you already solved for.
